The solution in [this comment](https://github.com/monero-project/research-lab/issues/70#issuecomment-768036260) appears to resolve the concerns raised by this issue.\r\n\r\nNOTE: Starting at [this comment](https://github.com/monero-project/research-lab/issues/70#issuecomment-1024964432) the discussion shifted from the original topic to questions about scaling and network stability.\r\n\r\nAs many people know, the fee algorithm has gone through various iterations. At one point, JollyMort performed an [extensive analysis](https://github.com/JollyMort/monero-research/blob/master/Monero\\%20Dynamic\\%20Block\\%20Size\\%20and\\%20Dynamic\\%20Minimum\\%20Fee/Monero\\%20Dynamic\\%20Block\\%20Size\\%20and\\%20Dynamic\\%20Minimum\\%20Fee\\%20-\\%20DRAFT.md) which led to our dynamic fee algorithm based on a 'reference' transaction, and since then long term block weights have been added to mitigate the [big bang attack](https://github.com/noncesense-research-lab/Blockchain_big_bang/blob/master/models/Isthmus_Bx_big_bang_model.ipynb). I believe there is still room for improvement.\r\n\r\n*Overview of current algorithms*\r\n\r\nPlease see [Zero to Monero: Second Edition](https://web.getmonero.org/library/Zero-to-Monero-2-0-0.pdf), sections 7.3.2, 7.3.3, and 7.3.4. As I understand it, @ArticMine is the architect of those algorithms.\r\n\r\n*Problem to be solved*\r\n\r\nImagine adoption is humming along and the long term median gets up really high, say 100x the current default penalty free zone (300kB, so we'd be at 30MB blocks [sic]). Suddenly catastrophe hits, and several major sources of transaction volume are taken offline (maybe some darknet markets were attacked by law enforcement, or perhaps it's world war 4 and some legal marketplaces get hit by EMPs). Short term transaction volume collapses to 5x the default penalty free zone, and now minimum fees are abruptly 20x higher. This is because per byte fees are divided by the minimum of short and long term medians.\r\n\r\nTransactions built before the short term median falls will be using the older fees, which will now be inadequate, and those tx will get stranded, even if they are using the 'normal' fee priority which is 5x the minimum fee.\r\n\r\nA similar thing could happen with much smaller volume shocks, to any transaction using the lowest fee priority (e.g. 1x the minimum).\r\n\r\nIt's not a problem if transaction volume never really exceeds the default penalty free zone, but design of the fee algorithm has always been forward looking so I don't see any reason to hold back.\r\n\r\n*Solution (OUTDATED, go to [this comment](https://github.com/monero-project/research-lab/issues/70#issuecomment-590135961))*\r\n\r\nSimply, make the minimum fee median `FM = max(300kB, long_term_median)`. Now it will only gradually change as the long term median changes.\r\n\r\nOf course, we must also change the penalty median since the fee is intended to afford one reference transaction's worth of penalty cost. Use the long term median `ML = max(300kB, median_100000_long_term_weights)` for penalty calculations instead of the cumulative median. But wait, this would seem to retract the upgrade for surge environments (we want some short term flexibility in block weights). The key insight here is making the 'penalty free zone' scale with the short term median, and the 'penalty zone' scale with long term median. Let's look at the penalty calculation (as it is done now; CM is the cumulative median `CM = max(300kB, min(median_100_blocks_weights, 50*ML))`).\r\n\r\n`P = B*(block_weight/CM - 1)^2`\r\n\r\nNote that the penalty only activates when block_weight \u003e CM. We can reorganize it:\r\n\r\n`P = B*([block_weight - CM]/CM)^2`\r\n\r\nWe want the 'activation' to happen when block weights are larger than the cumulative median, while the penalty itself scales with the long term median.\r\n\r\n`P = B*([block_weight - CM]/ML)^2`\r\n\r\nAnd the maximum block weight is `MAX = CM + ML` (instead of `MAX = 2*CM` which we have now).\r\n\r\nThe penalty to add one transaction above the cumulative median will slowly change as the long term median changes, but the penalty free zone is still free to fluctuate relatively rapidly. This also greatly increases the cost to set up a spam attack, as attackers will pay a fixed rate per byte to increase the short term median, rather than a fixed rate per percentage of the penalty zone (which becomes equivalent to more and more bytes as the short term median rises, with our current algorithms). It also ingrains this anti-spam mechanism directly into the penalty calculation, rather than the fee algorithm which is technically optional for nodes (it is network consensus, not protocol consensus, to enforce the minimum fee).\r\n\r\n*Changing long term median to long term average*\r\n\r\nThe long term median is meant to reflect a large volume of transaction history, yet it can also change quite abruptly if short term volume shocks turn into long term volume shocks. Suppose transaction volume is chugging along at a high rate for quite a while, then after our catastrophe it halves semi-permanently. 35 days later the long term median will suffer a rapid adjustment, which seems to defy its supposed 'long term' nature. A similar thing could happen in the opposite direction with a sudden 40% rise in transaction volume. By making it a long term average, adjustments to changing overall transaction volume would be 'priced in' much more gradually.\r\n\r\nIt makes sense to keep our short term median, a median, since it works quite well for ignoring outliers. There are no meaningful outliers over 100000 blocks.\r\n\r\n*Reducing granularity: the construction-publish time delta heuristic*\r\n\r\nTransaction authors always base their tx fees off the current blockchain state, yet it can take some time before the tx actually gets mined into a block. Observers can compare the fee included, to the expected fee for a tx's resident block, to estimate the [time delta](https://usercontent.irccloud-cdn.com/file/4SMYpo99/image.png) (image credit: @Isthmus) between tx creation and being mined. That heuristic may be useful to fingerprint different kinds of users. At one point, JollyMort performed an \u003ca href=\"https://github.com/JollyMort/monero-research/blob/master/Monero%20Dynamic%20Block%20Size%20and%20Dynamic%20Minimum%20Fee/Monero%20Dynamic%20Block%20Size%20and%20Dynamic%20Minimum%20Fee%20-%20DRAFT.md\"\u003eextensive analysis\u003c/a\u003e which led to our dynamic fee algorithm based on a 'reference' transaction, and since then long term block weights have been added to mitigate the \u003ca href=\"https://github.com/noncesense-research-lab/Blockchain_big_bang/blob/master/models/Isthmus_Bx_big_bang_model.ipynb\"\u003ebig bang attack\u003c/a\u003e. I believe there is still room for improvement.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003cem\u003eOverview of current algorithms\u003c/em\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003ePlease see \u003ca href=\"https://web.getmonero.org/library/Zero-to-Monero-2-0-0.pdf\" rel=\"nofollow\"\u003eZero to Monero: Second Edition\u003c/a\u003e, sections 7.3.2, 7.3.3, and 7.3.4. As I understand it, \u003ca class=\"user-mention notranslate\" data-hovercard-type=\"user\" data-hovercard-url=\"/users/ArticMine/hovercard\" data-octo-click=\"hovercard-link-click\" data-octo-dimensions=\"link_type:self\" href=\"https://github.com/ArticMine\"\u003e@ArticMine\u003c/a\u003e is the architect of those algorithms.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003cem\u003eProblem to be solved\u003c/em\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eImagine adoption is humming along and the long term median gets up really high, say 100x the current default penalty free zone (300kB, so we'd be at 30MB blocks [sic]). Suddenly catastrophe hits, and several major sources of transaction volume are taken offline (maybe some darknet markets were attacked by law enforcement, or perhaps it's world war 4 and some legal marketplaces get hit by EMPs). Short term transaction volume collapses to 5x the default penalty free zone, and now minimum fees are abruptly 20x higher. This is because per byte fees are divided by the minimum of short and long term medians.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eTransactions built before the short term median falls will be using the older fees, which will now be inadequate, and those tx will get stranded, even if they are using the 'normal' fee priority which is 5x the minimum fee.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eA similar thing could happen with much smaller volume shocks, to any transaction using the lowest fee priority (e.g. 1x the minimum).\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eIt's not a problem if transaction volume never really exceeds the default penalty free zone, but design of the fee algorithm has always been forward looking so I don't see any reason to hold back.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003cem\u003eSolution (OUTDATED, go to \u003ca href=\"https://github.com/monero-project/research-lab/issues/70#issuecomment-590135961\" data-hovercard-type=\"issue\" data-hovercard-url=\"/monero-project/research-lab/issues/70/hovercard\"\u003ethis comment\u003c/a\u003e)\u003c/em\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eSimply, make the minimum fee median \u003ccode class=\"notranslate\"\u003eFM = max(300kB, long_term_median)\u003c/code\u003e. Now it will only gradually change as the long term median changes.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eOf course, we must also change the penalty median since the fee is intended to afford one reference transaction's worth of penalty cost. Use the long term median \u003ccode class=\"notranslate\"\u003eML = max(300kB, median_100000_long_term_weights)\u003c/code\u003e for penalty calculations instead of the cumulative median. But wait, this would seem to retract the upgrade for surge environments (we want some short term flexibility in block weights). The key insight here is making the 'penalty free zone' scale with the short term median, and the 'penalty zone' scale with long term median. Let's look at the penalty calculation (as it is done now; CM is the cumulative median \u003ccode class=\"notranslate\"\u003eCM = max(300kB, min(median_100_blocks_weights, 50*ML))\u003c/code\u003e).\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003ccode class=\"notranslate\"\u003eP = B*(block_weight/CM - 1)^2\u003c/code\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eNote that the penalty only activates when block_weight \u0026gt; CM. We can reorganize it:\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003ccode class=\"notranslate\"\u003eP = B*([block_weight - CM]/CM)^2\u003c/code\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eWe want the 'activation' to happen when block weights are larger than the cumulative median, while the penalty itself scales with the long term median.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003ccode class=\"notranslate\"\u003eP = B*([block_weight - CM]/ML)^2\u003c/code\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eAnd the maximum block weight is \u003ccode class=\"notranslate\"\u003eMAX = CM + ML\u003c/code\u003e (instead of \u003ccode class=\"notranslate\"\u003eMAX = 2*CM\u003c/code\u003e which we have now).\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eThe penalty to add one transaction above the cumulative median will slowly change as the long term median changes, but the penalty free zone is still free to fluctuate relatively rapidly. This also greatly increases the cost to set up a spam attack, as attackers will pay a fixed rate per byte to increase the short term median, rather than a fixed rate per percentage of the penalty zone (which becomes equivalent to more and more bytes as the short term median rises, with our current algorithms). It also ingrains this anti-spam mechanism directly into the penalty calculation, rather than the fee algorithm which is technically optional for nodes (it is network consensus, not protocol consensus, to enforce the minimum fee).\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003cem\u003eChanging long term median to long term average\u003c/em\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eThe long term median is meant to reflect a large volume of transaction history, yet it can also change quite abruptly if short term volume shocks turn into long term volume shocks. Suppose transaction volume is chugging along at a high rate for quite a while, then after our catastrophe it halves semi-permanently. 35 days later the long term median will suffer a rapid adjustment, which seems to defy its supposed 'long term' nature. A similar thing could happen in the opposite direction with a sudden 40% rise in transaction volume. By making it a long term average, adjustments to changing overall transaction volume would be 'priced in' much more gradually.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eIt makes sense to keep our short term median, a median, since it works quite well for ignoring outliers. At one point, JollyMort performed an [extensive analysis](https://github.com/JollyMort/monero-research/blob/master/Monero\\%20Dynamic\\%20Block\\%20Size\\%20and\\%20Dynamic\\%20Minimum\\%20Fee/Monero\\%20Dynamic\\%20Block\\%20Size\\%20and\\%20Dynamic\\%20Minimum\\%20Fee\\%20-\\%20DRAFT.md) which led to our dynamic fee algorithm based on a 'reference' transaction, and since then long term block weights have been added to mitigate the [big bang attack](https://github.com/noncesense-research-lab/Blockchain_big_bang/blob/master/models/Isthmus_Bx_big_bang_model.ipynb). I believe there is still room for improvement.\r\n\r\n*Overview of current algorithms*\r\n\r\nPlease see [Zero to Monero: Second Edition](https://web.getmonero.org/library/Zero-to-Monero-2-0-0.pdf), sections 7.3.2, 7.3.3, and 7.3.4. As I understand it, @ArticMine is the architect of those algorithms.\r\n\r\n*Problem to be solved*\r\n\r\nImagine adoption is humming along and the long term median gets up really high, say 100x the current default penalty free zone (300kB, so we'd be at 30MB blocks [sic]). Suddenly catastrophe hits, and several major sources of transaction volume are taken offline (maybe some darknet markets were attacked by law enforcement, or perhaps it's world war 4 and some legal marketplaces get hit by EMPs). Short term transaction volume collapses to 5x the default penalty free zone, and now minimum fees are abruptly 20x higher. This is because per byte fees are divided by the minimum of short and long term medians.\r\n\r\nTransactions built before the short term median falls will be using the older fees, which will now be inadequate, and those tx will get stranded, even if they are using the 'normal' fee priority which is 5x the minimum fee.\r\n\r\nA similar thing could happen with much smaller volume shocks, to any transaction using the lowest fee priority (e.g. 1x the minimum).\r\n\r\nIt's not a problem if transaction volume never really exceeds the default penalty free zone, but design of the fee algorithm has always been forward looking so I don't see any reason to hold back.\r\n\r\n*Solution (OUTDATED, go to [this comment](https://github.com/monero-project/research-lab/issues/70#issuecomment-590135961))*\r\n\r\nSimply, make the minimum fee median `FM = max(300kB, long_term_median)`. Now it will only gradually change as the long term median changes.\r\n\r\nOf course, we must also change the penalty median since the fee is intended to afford one reference transaction's worth of penalty cost. Use the long term median `ML = max(300kB, median_100000_long_term_weights)` for penalty calculations instead of the cumulative median. But wait, this would seem to retract the upgrade for surge environments (we want some short term flexibility in block weights). The key insight here is making the 'penalty free zone' scale with the short term median, and the 'penalty zone' scale with long term median. Let's look at the penalty calculation (as it is done now; CM is the cumulative median `CM = max(300kB, min(median_100_blocks_weights, 50*ML))`).\r\n\r\n`P = B*(block_weight/CM - 1)^2`\r\n\r\nNote that the penalty only activates when block_weight > CM. We can reorganize it:\r\n\r\n`P = B*([block_weight - CM]/CM)^2`\r\n\r\nWe want the 'activation' to happen when block weights are larger than the cumulative median, while the penalty itself scales with the long term median.\r\n\r\n`P = B*([block_weight - CM]/ML)^2`\r\n\r\nAnd the maximum block weight is `MAX = CM + ML` (instead of `MAX = 2*CM` which we have now).\r\n\r\nThe penalty to add one transaction above the cumulative median will slowly change as the long term median changes, but the penalty free zone is still free to fluctuate relatively rapidly. This also greatly increases the cost to set up a spam attack, as attackers will pay a fixed rate per byte to increase the short term median, rather than a fixed rate per percentage of the penalty zone (which becomes equivalent to more and more bytes as the short term median rises, with our current algorithms). It also ingrains this anti-spam mechanism directly into the penalty calculation, rather than the fee algorithm which is technically optional for nodes (it is network consensus, not protocol consensus, to enforce the minimum fee).\r\n\r\n*Changing long term median to long term average*\r\n\r\nThe long term median is meant to reflect a large volume of transaction history, yet it can also change quite abruptly if short term volume shocks turn into long term volume shocks. Suppose transaction volume is chugging along at a high rate for quite a while, then after our catastrophe it halves semi-permanently. 35 days later the long term median will suffer a rapid adjustment, which seems to defy its supposed 'long term' nature. A similar thing could happen in the opposite direction with a sudden 40% rise in transaction volume. By making it a long term average, adjustments to changing overall transaction volume would be 'priced in' much more gradually.\r\n\r\nIt makes sense to keep our short term median, a median, since it works quite well for ignoring outliers. There are no meaningful outliers over 100000 blocks.\r\n\r\n*Reducing granularity: the construction-publish time delta heuristic*\r\n\r\nTransaction authors always base their tx fees off the current blockchain state, yet it can take some time before the tx actually gets mined into a block. Observers can compare the fee included, to the expected fee for a tx's resident block, to estimate the [time delta](https://usercontent.irccloud-cdn.com/file/4SMYpo99/image.png) (image credit: @Isthmus) between tx creation and being mined. That heuristic may be useful to fingerprint different kinds of users. Note that this heuristic also applies to age of the youngest ring member, so rounding fees like this doesn't completely solve the problem.\r\n\r\nWe can do simple rounding on the minimum fee, which already changes only slowly over the course of a single day (assuming my updated fee using long term average), to reduce the granularity of the time delta heuristic. Fewer significant digits equates to less granularity.\r\n\r\nSuppose we want to round up to `N` significant digits, `F` is the explicitly calculated fee, and we are doing integer arithmetic. Find the order of magnitude of `F` (i.e. number of decimal digits), `N_f`, then calculate\r\n\r\n```\r\nthrow_away = F % 10^(N_f - N);\r\n\r\nif (throw_away > 0) then\r\n{\r\nF -= throw_away;\r\nF += 10^(N_f - N);\t\r\n}\r\n```","author":{"url":"https://github.com/UkoeHB","@type":"Person","name":"UkoeHB"},"datePublished":"2020-02-16T21:38:42Z","url":"https://github.com/monero-project/research-lab/issues/70"}</script><div data-team-hovercards-enabled="true" class="markdown-body" data-turbolinks="false"><div class="markdown-body safe-html-box__Uwc6Al"><p dir="auto">STATUS: The solution in <a href="https://github.com/monero-project/research-lab/issues/70#issuecomment-768036260" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/monero-project/research-lab/issues/70/hovercard">this comment</a> appears to resolve the concerns raised by this issue.</p>
<p dir="auto">NOTE: Starting at <a href="https://github.com/monero-project/research-lab/issues/70#issuecomment-1024964432" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/monero-project/research-lab/issues/70/hovercard">this comment</a> the discussion shifted from the original topic to questions about scaling and network stability.</p>
<p dir="auto">As many people know, the fee algorithm has gone through various iterations. At one point, JollyMort performed an <a href="https://github.com/JollyMort/monero-research/blob/master/Monero%20Dynamic%20Block%20Size%20and%20Dynamic%20Minimum%20Fee/Monero%20Dynamic%20Block%20Size%20and%20Dynamic%20Minimum%20Fee%20-%20DRAFT.md">extensive analysis</a> which led to our dynamic fee algorithm based on a 'reference' transaction, and since then long term block weights have been added to mitigate the <a href="https://github.com/noncesense-research-lab/Blockchain_big_bang/blob/master/models/Isthmus_Bx_big_bang_model.ipynb">big bang attack</a>. I believe there is still room for improvement.</p>
<p dir="auto"><em>Overview of current algorithms</em></p>
<p dir="auto">Please see <a href="https://web.getmonero.org/library/Zero-to-Monero-2-0-0.pdf" rel="nofollow">Zero to Monero: Second Edition</a>, sections 7.3.2, 7.3.3, and 7.3.4. As I understand it, <a class="user-mention notranslate" data-hovercard-type="user" data-hovercard-url="/users/ArticMine/hovercard" data-octo-click="hovercard-link-click" data-octo-dimensions="link_type:self" href="https://github.com/ArticMine">@ArticMine</a> is the architect of those algorithms.</p>
<p dir="auto"><em>Problem to be solved</em></p>
<p dir="auto">Imagine adoption is humming along and the long term median gets up really high, say 100x the current default penalty free zone (300kB, so we'd be at 30MB blocks [sic]). Suddenly catastrophe hits, and several major sources of transaction volume are taken offline (maybe some darknet markets were attacked by law enforcement, or perhaps it's world war 4 and some legal marketplaces get hit by EMPs). Short term transaction volume collapses to 5x the default penalty free zone, and now minimum fees are abruptly 20x higher. This is because per byte fees are divided by the minimum of short and long term medians.</p>
<p dir="auto">Transactions built before the short term median falls will be using the older fees, which will now be inadequate, and those tx will get stranded, even if they are using the 'normal' fee priority which is 5x the minimum fee.</p>
<p dir="auto">A similar thing could happen with much smaller volume shocks, to any transaction using the lowest fee priority (e.g. 1x the minimum).</p>
<p dir="auto">It's not a problem if transaction volume never really exceeds the default penalty free zone, but design of the fee algorithm has always been forward looking so I don't see any reason to hold back.</p>
<p dir="auto"><em>Solution (OUTDATED, go to <a href="https://github.com/monero-project/research-lab/issues/70#issuecomment-590135961" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/monero-project/research-lab/issues/70/hovercard">this comment</a>)</em></p>
<p dir="auto">Simply, make the minimum fee median <code class="notranslate">FM = max(300kB, long_term_median)</code>. Now it will only gradually change as the long term median changes.</p>
<p dir="auto">Of course, we must also change the penalty median since the fee is intended to afford one reference transaction's worth of penalty cost. Use the long term median <code class="notranslate">ML = max(300kB, median_100000_long_term_weights)</code> for penalty calculations instead of the cumulative median. But wait, this would seem to retract the upgrade for surge environments (we want some short term flexibility in block weights). The key insight here is making the 'penalty free zone' scale with the short term median, and the 'penalty zone' scale with long term median. Let's look at the penalty calculation (as it is done now; CM is the cumulative median <code class="notranslate">CM = max(300kB, min(median_100_blocks_weights, 50*ML))</code>).</p>
<p dir="auto"><code class="notranslate">P = B*(block_weight/CM - 1)^2</code></p>
<p dir="auto">Note that the penalty only activates when block_weight > CM. We can reorganize it:</p>
<p dir="auto"><code class="notranslate">P = B*([block_weight - CM]/CM)^2</code></p>
<p dir="auto">We want the 'activation' to happen when block weights are larger than the cumulative median, while the penalty itself scales with the long term median.</p>
<p dir="auto"><code class="notranslate">P = B*([block_weight - CM]/ML)^2</code></p>
<p dir="auto">And the maximum block weight is <code class="notranslate">MAX = CM + ML</code> (instead of <code class="notranslate">MAX = 2*CM</code> which we have now).</p>
<p dir="auto">The penalty to add one transaction above the cumulative median will slowly change as the long term median changes, but the penalty free zone is still free to fluctuate relatively rapidly. This also greatly increases the cost to set up a spam attack, as attackers will pay a fixed rate per byte to increase the short term median, rather than a fixed rate per percentage of the penalty zone (which becomes equivalent to more and more bytes as the short term median rises, with our current algorithms). It also ingrains this anti-spam mechanism directly into the penalty calculation, rather than the fee algorithm which is technically optional for nodes (it is network consensus, not protocol consensus, to enforce the minimum fee).</p>
<p dir="auto"><em>Changing long term median to long term average</em></p>
<p dir="auto">The long term median is meant to reflect a large volume of transaction history, yet it can also change quite abruptly if short term volume shocks turn into long term volume shocks. Suppose transaction volume is chugging along at a high rate for quite a while, then after our catastrophe it halves semi-permanently. 35 days later the long term median will suffer a rapid adjustment, which seems to defy its supposed 'long term' nature. A similar thing could happen in the opposite direction with a sudden 40% rise in transaction volume. By making it a long term average, adjustments to changing overall transaction volume would be 'priced in' much more gradually.</p>
<p dir="auto">It makes sense to keep our short term median, a median, since it works quite well for ignoring outliers. There are no meaningful outliers over 100000 blocks.</p>
<p dir="auto"><em>Reducing granularity: the construction-publish time delta heuristic</em></p>
<p dir="auto">Transaction authors always base their tx fees off the current blockchain state, yet it can take some time before the tx actually gets mined into a block. Observers can compare the fee included, to the expected fee for a tx's resident block, to estimate the <a href="https://usercontent.irccloud-cdn.com/file/4SMYpo99/image.png" rel="nofollow">time delta</a> (image credit: <a class="user-mention notranslate" data-hovercard-type="user" data-hovercard-url="/users/Isthmus/hovercard" data-octo-click="hovercard-link-click" data-octo-dimensions="link_type:self" href="https://github.com/Isthmus">@Isthmus</a>) between tx creation and being mined. That heuristic may be useful to fingerprint different kinds of users. Note that this heuristic also applies to age of the youngest ring member, so rounding fees like this doesn't completely solve the problem.</p>
<p dir="auto">We can do simple rounding on the minimum fee, which already changes only slowly over the course of a single day (assuming my updated fee using long term average), to reduce the granularity of the time delta heuristic. Fewer significant digits equates to less granularity.</p>
<p dir="auto">Suppose we want to round up to <code class="notranslate">N</code> significant digits, <code class="notranslate">F</code> is the explicitly calculated fee, and we are doing integer arithmetic. Find the order of magnitude of <code class="notranslate">F</code> (i.e. number of decimal digits), <code class="notranslate">N_f</code>, then calculate</p>

<p dir="auto">Re: Proposed Scaling Definitions (January 2021)</p>
<p dir="auto">EDITED</p>
<ol dir="auto">
<li>This line threw me off quite a bit <code class="notranslate">M_L ; Penalty free zone. This is now dynamic.</code> It looks like in fact the penalty free zone and penalty zone are the same, which seems acceptable to me.</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto">However, I still believe a long term average instead of median would be better. If a shock event causes transaction volume to fall, then 69 days later the long term median will abruptly plummet. Tx made with low fees before that drop-off will get stranded. It means tx authors have to be aware that minimum tx fees will rise, which is sub-optimal from a UX perspective (compared to tx authors being more-or-less oblivious to the state of the network).</p>
<ol start="2" dir="auto">
<li>
<p dir="auto">Minimum fee changes look fine to me.</p>
</li>
<li>
<p dir="auto">It is not clear what the 10 block buffer for wallet fees is for.</p>
</li>
<li>
<p dir="auto">I recommend a default policy of two significant digits for fee rounding.</p>
</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto">Overall I believe the proposed changes resolve the concerns raised by this issue.</p></div></div><div role="toolbar" aria-label="Reactions" class="d-flex gap-1 data-turbolinks="false"><div class="markdown-body safe-html-box__Uwc6Al"><p dir="auto">First many thanks to <a class="user-mention notranslate" data-hovercard-type="user" data-hovercard-url="/users/UkoeHB/hovercard" data-octo-click="hovercard-link-click" data-octo-dimensions="link_type:self" href="https://github.com/UkoeHB">@UkoeHB</a> for your work in reviewing this proposal. Also many thanks to all those who commented and made suggestions.</p>
<p dir="auto">I updated the definition to clarify the calculation of the wallet fees. There is no need for a second recursion calculation for the wallet fee medians. <a href="https://github.com/ArticMine/Monero-Documents/blob/master/MoneroScaling2021-02.pdf">https://github.com/ArticMine/Monero-Documents/blob/master/MoneroScaling2021-02.pdf</a></p>
<p dir="auto">The 10 block buffer is designed to address a change in fees between the time a transaction, for immediate broadcast is, assembled, broadcast and relayed.</p>
<p dir="auto">With respect to the cap I considered 1.6 / 0.625, 2 / 0.5 and 2.5 / 0.4.  I considered transaction rate changes not only in Monero but also Bitcoin (before the limit was reached), Litecoin, Dogecoin, Dash, and Bitcoin Cash. Here is a chart for Monero, Bitcoin and Litecoin. <a href="https://bitinfocharts.com/comparison/transactions-btc-ltc-xmr.html#log" rel="nofollow">https://bitinfocharts.com/comparison/transactions-btc-ltc-xmr.html#log</a>. Increases of 8x over a six month period and even 80x over a 1 year period have occurred in the past and can occur in the future. This is especially the case if there is a disruption in a competing coin as occurred in 2017 with Bitcoin reaching a hard limit triggering an 80x increase in Litecoin transactions. Setting this cap below 2 does run the real risk of triggering this issue if one allows the short term median to remain above the long term median for many months. On the other hand increasing the limit to say 2.5 / 0.4 would lead to a much larger spread in fees. There is also little evidence for uncontrolled growth over multiple years even in chains with no penalty to increase the blocksize below the hard cap such as Litecoin. One can take a look at Litecoin transactions in 2018 or Monero transactions in early 2017 for example. Also it is best to use figures where the reciprocal can be expressed as an exact decimal. 2 / 0.5 vs say 1.7 / 0.58823529... .</p></div></div><div role="toolbar" aria-label="Reactions" class="d-flex not been adequately addressed. I also have <a href="https://github.com/monero-project/research-lab/issues/91#issuecomment-1018641072" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/monero-project/research-lab/issues/91/hovercard">some concerns</a> about scaling.</p>
<p dir="auto">To summarize:</p>
<ol dir="auto">
<li><strong>Spam cost</strong>: If the dynamic block size can expand at a fast rate, then it could theoretically balloon to massive levels due to a spam attack. Higher rates of expansion mean lower cost to the spammer (and more rapid results). <a class="user-mention notranslate" data-hovercard-type="user" data-hovercard-url="/users/ArticMine/hovercard" data-octo-click="hovercard-link-click" data-octo-dimensions="link_type:self" href="https://github.com/ArticMine">@ArticMine</a> 's <a href="https://github.com/monero-project/monero/pull/7819" data-hovercard-type="pull_request" data-hovercard-url="/monero-project/monero/pull/7819/hovercard">fee changes</a> would increase the maximum rate of long-term-median growth from 1.4x over 69 days to 2x, which is a maximal change of 5x vs 32x over 1 year. Note that the short-term median can rise to 50x over the long-term median, which means the absolute upper limit on block size after 1 year of maximal long-term growth would be 250x vs 1600x.<br>
a. If we start at 300kB blocks, this means 1.5MB vs 9.6MB long-term median-sized blocks (1k vs 6.5k tx per block [for ~1.4kB 2-in/2-out tx], or 8.3 vs 54.2 tx/sec), and 75MB vs 480MB maximal short-term-median blocks (50k vs 325k tx per block, or 415 vs 2710 tx/sec).<br>
b. TODO: what is the actual cost of a spam attack with these numbers?</li>
<li><strong>Network stability</strong>: Nodes are resource-constrained, they have bandwidth limits (kB/sec) and CPU-time limits (tx verified per second).<br>
a. If a node can't download or verify new blocks as fast as they appear, then they will fall behind the network. Users would only be able to rely on fast nodes in order to get a fresh view of the blockchain.<br>
b. A related problem is block-verification-times will start to factor into mining profitability. It would give mining pools a significant advantage over solo-miners.<br>
c. If a node wants to re-validate the blockchain, but their computer isn't able to catch up to the top of the chain within a reasonable time-span (because the chain tip is moving too fast relative to their verification speed), then it is basically infeasible to re-validate the chain for many users. That point will be reached eventually regardless of chain tip speed, because new blocks always increase the static cost of re-validation. However, a fast moving chain tip makes the problem even worse (and makes it occur far sooner).<br>
d. According to my <a href="https://github.com/monero-project/research-lab/issues/91" data-hovercard-type="issue" data-hovercard-url="/monero-project/research-lab/issues/91/hovercard">performance research</a> into Seraphis, one thread on a high-end CPU can verify about 167 CLSAG 2-in/2-out 11-ring-size txs per second. A mid-range CPU with a busy thread scheduler can probably do half that, at best. Moving to 16-ring-size CLSAG or 128-ring-size Seraphis would further reduce that number by 30-50%.</li>
</ol></div></div><div role="toolbar" aria-label="Reactions" class="d-flex gap-1 flex-wrap"></div></div></div></div></div></div></div></li><li data-wrapper-timeline-id="IC_kwDOArRvmc49HVwM"><div class="markdown-body" data-turbolinks="false"><div class="markdown-body safe-html-box__Uwc6Al"><p dir="auto">It is possible to implement the proposal including the proposed fees using 1.7 and 1/1.7 rather than 2 and 1/2. This fee structure works because it is using a less responsive ML of 1.7 with the fee spreads of the more responsive ML of 2. I am proposing we proceed for the upcoming HF with a 1.7 per cycle growth rate. Changing 2 to 1.7 for the growth rate of ML is the only change.</p>
<p dir="auto">The following equations would be change from:</p>
<p dir="auto">ML = The median over the last 100000 blocks of max((min(MB , 2ML), ZM , ML/2) ; recursive calculation for ML with ML starting at ML of previous 100001 block (currently = ZM);</p>
<p dir="auto">MLW = The median over the last 99990 blocks and future 10blocks (100000 blocks) of max((min (MBW , 2ML), ZM ,ML/2)</p>
<p dir="auto">to:</p>
<p dir="auto">ML = The median over the last 100000 blocks of max((min(MB , 1.7ML), ZM , ML/1.7) ; recursive calculation for ML with ML starting at ML of previous 100001 block (currently = ZM);</p>
<p dir="auto">MLW = The median over the last 99990 blocks and future 10blocks (100000 blocks) of max((min (MBW , 1.7ML), ZM ,ML/1.7)</p>
<p dir="auto">This implements what <a class="user-mention notranslate" data-hovercard-type="user" data-hovercard-url="/users/SamsungGalaxyPlayer/hovercard" data-octo-click="hovercard-link-click" data-octo-dimensions="link_type:self" href="https://github.com/SamsungGalaxyPlayer">@SamsungGalaxyPlayer</a> proposed as a compromise,</p>
<p dir="auto">While this does not fully address, in my view, the responsiveness of ML over a 2 - 5  month period it does address everything else in the issue. This of course is a major improvement over the current situation and does address over 90%, but not all, of my concerns with the current situation</p>
<p dir="auto">This allows time in order to reach final consensus on the question of 1.7 vs 2 rate of growth per cycle for ML for the subsequent HF. It also allow for a proper analysis and discussion of the scaling questions that have been raised.before reaching a final consensus on ML.</p></div></div><div role="toolbar" aria-label="Reactions" data-turbolinks="false"><div class="markdown-body safe-html-box__Uwc6Al"><p dir="auto">It's probably not realistic to consider this absolute worst case scenario as an attack, because the attacker would have to pay a monumental amount of fees to overcome the penalty inflicted on the "rational miner". Calculating those costs should be a priority though and they should ideally be on the same order of magnitude as a 51% attack, even for non-maximised growth rates. As a consequence of global adoption though I think it is a concern. I see no disincentive for miners allowing blocks to grow beyond a size where verifying consumer hardware nodes can catch up (other than their own additional accelerating storage costs).</p>
<p dir="auto">I remember reading in the MRL channel long ago that Monero DOES in fact have a "sanity check" type maximum blocksize somewhere in the code. However, I was unable to find what this currently is or verify my memory of someone saying there is a hardcap. If this is the case it should probably be tweaked to a size using calculations like the ones in the spreadsheet but referencing much lower spec hardware, and bearing in mind that many nodes will not have multiple TB of storage space right now.</p>
<p dir="auto">I'm glad that the tweaks to the PR result in a less scary maximum annual growth rate. However I'm of the opinion that fees are still generally too low. It is completely unacceptable that someone was able to bloat the chain by 700mb for $1000 (<a href="https://mitchellpkt.medium.com/fingerprinting-a-flood-forensic-statistical-analysis-of-the-mid-2021-monero-transaction-volume-a19cbf41ce60" rel="nofollow">https://mitchellpkt.medium.com/fingerprinting-a-flood-forensic-statistical-analysis-of-the-mid-2021-monero-transaction-volume-a19cbf41ce60</a>). Making the most private digital payment possible should be perceived as worth more than a fraction of a penny. A marginal increase in fees (e.g. from a fraction of a penny to roughly a penny) has almost no impact on the average user. It only impacts huge volume players/exchanges (which are themselves a centralizing factor and presumably generate profits to offset this) and spammers.</p>
<p dir="auto">I also agree with <a class="user-mention notranslate" data-hovercard-type="user" data-hovercard-url="/users/SamsungGalaxyPlayer/hovercard" data-octo-click="hovercard-link-click" data-octo-dimensions="link_type:self" href="https://github.com/SamsungGalaxyPlayer">@SamsungGalaxyPlayer</a> that avoiding a fee market at all costs is nonsensical. We are not BTC and we do not need to rely on a fee market because of tail emission, but we also don't need to avoid it entirely at the cost of irreversible bloat.</p>
<p dir="auto">A related thought I had is do we know for sure that miner implementations are actually set up to behave "rationally" once we are in the dynamic blocksize regime? i.e. does software like XMRig account for the penalty that will be applied correctly and allow itself to build blocks larger than 300kb under optimal fee environments, or does it naively just keep adding highest-fee transactions beyond the 300kb limit? It seems to me that if the mining software is not set up to actually figure this stuff out, the whole dynamic blocksize system will not kick in smoothly.</p>
<p dir="auto">There should probably also be an incentive for DECREASING the block size over time if the transaction volume allows it (unless there already is such an incentive and I've missed it).</p>
<p dir="auto">Please forgive my rambling comment.</p></div></div><div role="toolbar" aria-label="Reactions" class="d-flex gap-1 flex-wrap"></div></div></div></div></div></div></div></li><li class="markdown-body" data-turbolinks="false"><div class="markdown-body safe-html-box__Uwc6Al"><p dir="auto">Here is an article, by Peter Rizun, on a fee market caused by orphan blocks in a stressed network.A Transaction Fee Market Exists Without a Block Size Limit <a href="https://www.bitcoinunlimited.info/resources/feemarket.pdf" rel="nofollow">https://www.bitcoinunlimited.info/resources/feemarket.pdf</a></p>
<p dir="auto">I would pay close attention on the result on page 12</p>
<blockquote>
<p dir="auto">Not unexpectedly, we showed that the cost of block space was proportional to both Bitcoin’s inflation rate, 𝑅/𝑇, and the amount of time it takes per uncompressed megabyte to propagate block solutions to the other miners, 1/𝛾𝐶.</p>
</blockquote>
<p dir="auto">In my view this works in Monero, but not in Bitcoin or Bitcoin Cash because of Monero's tail emission. One can think of the Rizun term as an additional term added to the penalty in Monero.</p>
<p dir="auto">Edit 1: The Rizun term would only come into play if the blocksize has grown so large as to impact the probability of orphan blocks</p>
<p dir="auto">Edit 2:</p>
<blockquote>
<p dir="auto">If pools see that a non-trivial volume of txs (and tx fees) are being lost due to slow nodes in the network, then they will have a clear incentive to offer/encourage users to directly upload their txs to them.</p>
</blockquote>
<p dir="auto">If the node relay fee is significantly above the real fee market (Monero penalty plus Rizun term) then I do agree with the above assessment. My point is that if the network is stressed to the point that a significant number of nodes cannot upload all the transactions, then there would be an impact on orphan blocks, and the Rizun term would be triggered. There would be little incentive for miners to circumvent the nodes and instead the miners could well demand additional fees. One situation where the above assessment would apply is if the ML is artificially suppressed causing fees to rise, which is one of the reasons why I have argued for 2 over 1,7 and even more over 1.4 .</p></div></div><div role="toolbar" aria-label="Reactions" class="d-flex gap-1 flex-wrap"></div></div></div></div></div></div></div></li><li data-wrapper-timeline-id="IC_kwDOArRvmc49UDte"><div
